title: Coffee Hydration Calculator 2026 | Does Coffee Dehydrate You?
h1: Does Coffee Dehydrate? The Real Facts About Caffeine and Hydration
description: Calculate the net hydration from your daily coffee habit. See how many mL of fluid you actually get from coffee, your estimated caffeine intake, and whether you're within the 400 mg/day safe limit. Updated 2026.
intro: The idea that coffee dehydrates you is one of the most persistent health myths. Research shows the opposite: because coffee is mostly water, its net effect on your fluid balance is positive. The caffeine in a standard cup (~95 mg) does have a mild diuretic effect, but your body retains roughly 90% of the fluid you drink. This calculator estimates your daily net hydration from coffee and your total caffeine load so you can see the numbers for yourself.
keyTakeaway: Coffee contributes ~90% of its volume as net hydration. The dehydration myth comes from confusing a mild, short-lived diuretic effect with actual fluid loss. At normal intake levels (under 4 cups/day), coffee hydrates.
useCases: Checking whether your 4-cup-a-day habit is pushing you over the 400 mg caffeine safety threshold
Understanding how much of your daily fluid target is already covered by your morning coffee

Settling the 'coffee doesn't count as water' debate with actual numbers

explanation:
## How It's Calculated

The formula has two parts: **net hydration** and **caffeine load**.

### Net Hydration

Research published in the *British Journal of Nutrition* (Killer et al., 2014) found that moderate coffee consumption (4 × 200 mL cups/day) produced no significant difference in total body water compared to the same volume of plain water. The body retains approximately 90% of the fluid from coffee, with the remaining ~10% lost via the mild diuretic effect of caffeine:

```
Net hydration (mL) = cups × mL_per_cup × 0.90
```

### Caffeine Estimate

A standard 8 oz (240 mL) brewed filter coffee contains roughly 70–140 mg of caffeine, with the average at around 95 mg. The formula uses:

```
Caffeine (mg) = cups × 95
```

Note: espresso has ~63 mg per 30 mL shot; instant coffee ~60 mg per 240 mL. The 95 mg figure is representative of drip/filter coffee.

### Safety Threshold

The FDA and European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) both identify **400 mg of caffeine per day** as the amount generally not associated with adverse effects in healthy adults. Above that threshold the calculator issues a warning.

## Why the Dehydration Myth Persists

The myth dates to a 1928 study that used large doses of caffeine given to people who had abstained from caffeine for days. Under those conditions, a transient diuretic effect was observed. In habitual coffee drinkers at normal doses, the effect is negligible — the body adapts quickly to regular caffeine intake.

## Disclaimer

This calculator provides a general estimate. Individual caffeine sensitivity varies. Pregnant individuals, people with certain heart conditions, and those on specific medications should consult a doctor about their caffeine intake.

faq.a: No. Studies — including the frequently cited Killer et al. (2014) trial in the *British Journal of Nutrition* — found that moderate coffee intake produces the same hydration as an equal volume of water. Caffeine has a mild, short-lived diuretic effect, but the fluid in the coffee more than compensates for it. Net result: coffee hydrates.

faq.q: How much of the water in coffee does my body actually absorb?
faq.a: Approximately 90%. Because caffeine slightly increases urine output, the retention rate is a few percent lower than plain water, but the difference is negligible at typical intake levels. A 240 mL cup contributes roughly 216 mL to your fluid balance.

faq.q: What is a safe daily caffeine limit?
faq.a: Both the FDA and EFSA set the threshold at 400 mg per day for healthy adults. That corresponds to roughly 4 standard cups (240 mL) of filter coffee. Pregnant individuals are advised to stay under 200 mg/day. Beyond 400 mg, side effects such as anxiety, insomnia, and elevated heart rate become more common.

faq.q: How much caffeine is in a shot of espresso vs. a regular coffee?
faq.a: A single espresso shot (~30 mL) contains around 63 mg of caffeine. A standard 240 mL (8 oz) drip coffee contains 70–140 mg, averaging around 95 mg. Counterintuitively, espresso has more caffeine per mL but less per serving. This calculator uses 95 mg/cup as a representative average for filter coffee.

No. Tea has the same net hydrating effect as coffee. Black tea has roughly 47 mg of caffeine per 240 mL cup — about half that of filter coffee — so the mild diuretic effect is even smaller. Green tea has even less.

faq.q: Should coffee count toward my daily water intake goal?
faq.a: Yes. The U.S. National Academies and NHS both acknowledge that all beverages — including coffee and tea — contribute to daily fluid intake. The common advice to drink 8 glasses of *water* is a simplification; total fluid from all sources (food included) is what matters.

faq.q: Can I replace all my water with coffee?
faq.a: Technically coffee hydrates, but it is not ideal as your sole fluid source. Very high coffee intake drives caffeine above safe limits well before you reach your hydration target. For an average 70 kg adult needing about 2.5 L/day, you would need 10+ cups, which would deliver nearly 1,000 mg of caffeine — more than double the safe limit. Drink water alongside your coffee.

faq.q: Does adding milk or sugar change the hydration calculation?
faq.a: Adding milk increases the fluid volume slightly, so your net hydration would be marginally higher than the calculator shows (since the calculator only counts the coffee itself). Sugar has a negligible effect on hydration. The caffeine estimate remains the same regardless of additives.

faq.q: Does tolerance to caffeine change how it affects hydration?
faq.a: Yes. Regular coffee drinkers develop a tolerance to caffeine's diuretic effect within a few days of consistent intake. For habitual drinkers, the diuretic effect is even smaller than the 10% assumed here, meaning the net hydration may be slightly better than this calculator estimates.
